subject: english-language
title: Building a Persuasive Paragraph
welcome_lead: Put techniques together into one strong paragraph.
meta_desc: KS3 English Language adventure on combining persuasive techniques in writing.
final_note: You can now stack persuasive techniques into a paragraph.

walkthroughs.body_html: Open with a hook (statistic, anecdote, question) and a clear topic sentence. The reader should know your point in seconds.
Use PEEL: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link. Stack techniques inside — emotive language, rhetorical question, triplet.
Swap 'walked' for 'marched' and 'said' for 'declared'. Strong power verbs add force and clarity to persuasive writing.

mcqs.q: What is overextension in child language?
options: Overextension is when children use very long words they don't understand.
When a child applies a word more broadly than adults do — e.g. calling all four-legged animals 'dog' before learning distinct categories.
Overextension is when children speak too loudly.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between voiced and voiceless sounds?
options: Voiced sounds are produced with vocal-fold vibration (/b/, /d/, /g/, /z/); voiceless sounds without it (/p/, /t/, /k/, /s/). You can feel the difference by putting a hand on your throat.
Voiced sounds are loud and voiceless sounds are whispered.
Voiced sounds use the lips; voiceless sounds use the tongue.

A group of words from a similar area of meaning — e.g. 'whisper, scream, mumble, shout' all belong to the semantic field of vocalisation.
